# INTERNATIONALIZATION OF HIGHER EDUCATION IN THE COUNTRIES OF THE GULF COOPERATION COUNCIL: IMPACT ON THE NATIONAL LANGUAGE

F A T I M A B A D R Y 201 9
## Abstract
Internationalization of higher education by the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) countries is inscribed in an overall transformation of the Arabian gulf region from mainly tribal communities to modern nations aspiring to become global leaders in the knowledge-based economies of the twenty-first century. In the last six decades, thanks to their oil wealth, GCC countries have made great strides in developing their social, economic and education infrastructures. They have expanded their educational system by embracing internationalization to provide greater gender equity, wider access, greater choice, and nurturing tolerance and appreciation of diversity. Internationalization is carried out by importing Western educational models, faculty and institutions, establishing partnerships with international higher education institutions and adopting English as a medium of instruction. A major challenge has been implementing language-ineducation policies that are grounded in the linguistic and social contexts of the region. This report discusses the impact of English as medium of instruction practices on Arabic literacy in the absence of explicit dual language policies designed to develop students' competencies in both English as an international language and Arabic as a medium of knowledge production in order to be aligned with official GCC national visions.
## Introduction
Internationalization of higher education (HE) includes movement of students, institutions, educational models and programs, faculty and administrators across national boundaries. By the turn of the twenty-first century, global rankings of institutions, branding, distance and online courses, franchising, establishing networks and using English as a medium of instruction (EMI) have also become part of internationalization processes (Spring 2015; THE, 2017). While there are many benefits associated with internationalization, EMI in non-anglophone regions remains controversial. Its supporters believe it is a shortcut to accessing the latest knowledge, thus enabling graduates to become drivers of their nations' economic development while its opponents argue that EMI devalues national languages in education, limits research production in the native language, and erodes national and cultural identities.
This report reviews internationalization practices of HE in the six countries of the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC): The Kingdom of Bahrain, the state of Kuwait, the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia (KSA), the Sultanate of Oman, the state of Qatar and the United Arab Emirates (UAE). It explores how internationalization practices have downplayed long-term consequences of EMI policies on Arabic development and how they are misaligned with national vision statements upholding the importance of the Arabic language and its historical significance to these countries' identities. It points to the need for explicit dual language policies that are grounded in the linguistic and social contexts of the region and aimed at developing students' competencies in English as an international language and Arabic as a medium of knowledge production in line with official GCC national visions.
### Internationalization of higher education in GCC countries
The classification of educational services as a commodity by the 1995 World Trade Organization's (WTO) General Agreement on Trade and Services (GATS) expanded the global trade in education and accelerated its internationalization (Spring, 2015). By the beginning of the twenty first century, the changing political
environment resulting from the 9/11 events in 2001, and later, Brexit, Trumpism, and the ascendance of nationalist and anti-immigration movements in Europe and the US, shifted its direction and led to a decrease in student mobility Westward and an increase in the movement of Western educational providers eastward. GCC countries are among the countries that have experienced this shift in the last two decades, as they have welcomed the import of HE services and models into their relatively young higher education landscape.
In the last six decades and thanks to their oil wealth, GCC countries have witnessed a radical transformation of their societies from mainly tribal communities to modern nations aspiring to become leaders in the knowledge-based economies of the twenty-first century globalized world. Higher education is one of the sectors that have experienced an impressive growth in a relatively short span. Indeed, the first public university, King Saud University in KSA, only dates back to 1957 followed by Kuwait University in 1966, Qatar University in 1973, United Arab Emirates University (UAEU) in 1976, Sultan Qaboos University (Oman) and University of Bahrain in 1986 (Badry and Willoughby, 2016). These universities were set up on the model of Arab universities mainly by academics from Egypt, Syria, Lebanon, Jordan and Iraq. But, by the end of the twentieth century, there was mounting criticism with the Arab university model's failure to produce graduates with skills required by the globalized labor markets of the knowledge-based economies. Another criticism came from American and European governments who accused education in the Muslim world of disseminating fundamentalist religious ideologies, intolerance and Islamist terrorism. In the aftermath the 9/11 events, Muslim countries were urged to implement reforms to modernize their educational systems in order to promote tolerance and universal (that is, Western) values (Moini et al. 2009).
To reform their public universities and improve quality, GCC governments turned to the West by encouraging partnerships with foreign institutions, inviting branch campuses and opening the educational market to privatization. The reforms were generally based on recommendations from international organizations such as the UNDP, the OECD and the World Bank (UNDP 2004, OECD, 2008) and were largely based on an economic model and human capital theory of education (Spring, 2015). Reforms called for the adoption of Western curricula, pedagogy, and assessment criteria benchmarked on international frameworks such as the European Qualifications Framework (EQF) and the Bologna Framework (European Framework for Higher Education Qualifications) (CAA, 2012). A key component of internationalization was the switch from Arabic to English as a medium of instruction (EMI) believed to be 'the primary tool for improving the quality of teaching and learning' (Barnawi and Al Hawsawi 2017, p. 213). Their design and implementation were entrusted to international consultancy groups, and expatriate faculty and university leaders who were Western educated and who formed the majority of academics (80% to 95 %) in the non-public universities (Hamdan, 2013; KHDA, 2016; Le Haa and Barnawi, 2015). In the 2000's, HE witnessed an extraordinary expansion, particularly in its non-public sector^(i) to meet increased demand from both nationals and children of expatriate residents settled in GCC countries to support their booming economies. ii Internationalization was accomplished through a number of processes. Bahrain, KSA, Kuwait and Oman favored creating partnerships between local institutions and Western universities while the UAE and Qatar also invited foreign institutions to open branch campuses, offering them substantial financial incentives. In addition, local rulers and wealthy nationals launched private institutions based on American university models across the region (Badry and Willoughby, 2016; Barnawi, 2017; Barnawi and Al Hawsawi, 2017; Hayes, 2018; Le Haa and Barnawi, 2015; Mahboob and Ilyas, 2017).
### Strategies and policies regulating internationalized higher education in GCC countries
Multiple decrees and practices have championed internationalization of HE to deal with global challenges. The approach to language prioritizes English teaching, based on the assumption that GCC graduates must develop advanced English communication skills to compete in an increasingly globalized labor market. For example, KSA's royal decrees #171 dated 14/08 2004 and #160 dated 02/05/2011 introduced English in preuniversity levels to prepare students for study in English at tertiary levels; and in 2015, the "*Education for * *Career*" ministerial program promoted English education for university and career (Barnawi et. al. 2017, p. 200). In Bahrain, the 2014-24 National Higher Education Strategy is a '[s]trategic engagement in higher education internationalization… in leveraging strong global partnerships to assist in advancing the quality and diversity of education at a faster pace.' Among its expected outcomes is to produce '[g]lobal citizens [that are] work-ready' (Higher Education Council. p. 38).iii The Qatari Strategic Plan 2017-2022 aims to enhance Qataris' potential to contribute effectively to the workforce and the Qatari community… (The Peninsula, 2017) and the UAE's national higher education strategy is to 'deliver a modern, global, educational model to Emirati students' (*Gulf News,* 2017).
Different approaches to implement these strategies are all founded on the premise that internationalization of HE (including EMI) is the shortest path to developing human resources capable of powering GCC knowledge economies. In KSA, universities and colleges are encouraged to sign contracts of cooperation and partnerships with international universities, and local entities may obtain international education franchises to open tertiary institutions locally (Barnawi et al. 2017; Hamdan, 2013). Similar arrangements are followed in Bahrain, Kuwait and Oman. In Qatar, the Qatar Foundation (QF)iv invited elite American universities (and other Western universities), such as Virginia Commonwealth University, Georgetown University, Carnegie Mellon, Cornel University, Northwestern University, Texas A & M, to open branch campuses in selected disciplines in the newly established Qatar Education City (Badry and Willoughby, 2016; Moini, et.al., 2009). In the UAE, there are multiple arrangements. The Emirate of Abu Dhabi adopted a similar model to that of Qatar with the invitation of New York University Abu Dhabi (NYUAD) and the Sorbonne but also encouraged the creation of several private universities. Dubai set up educational free zones such as the Knowledge Village and Dubai Academic City where branch campuses as well as private universities offer educational services.^(v) The Sharjah University City established in 1997 by the Ruler of Sharjah, housed private institutions set up on the American model.
Regardless of which process is followed, GCC internationalization strategies lack an explicit dual language-ineducation policy that balances between improving Arabic and English language skills. The adoption of English as a medium of instruction, (and not as a foreign/second language), is not paired with practical solutions to improve Arabic competencies, despite widespread recognition that GCC students' Arabic literacy levels are on the decline. Such approaches are misaligned with GCC declarations that emphasize the importance of the Arabic language and culture as a pillar of national identity. For instance, the KSA vision 2030 aims 'to strengthen, preserve and highlight [its] national identity so that it can guide the lives of future generations. … by keeping true to [its] national values and principles, as well as by encouraging social development and upholding the Arabic language' (KSA Vision, 2030). The Oman educational council in its philosophy of education (Oman Vision, 2017, p. 20) states that: 'Citizenship involves a feeling of belongingness to the country and to its Arabic and Islamic identity.' Similarly, Qatar National Vision 2030 affirms that: 'Despite rapid economic and social gains, as well as political change, Qatar has maintained its cultural and traditional values as an Arab and Islamic nation …' (QNV 2008, p.1), and the UAE asserts in its 2021 vision that 'Arabic
will re-emerge as a dynamic and vibrant language, expressed everywhere in speech and writing as a living symbol of the nation's progressive Arab-Islamic values' (UAE Vision 2021, p. 4).
## Challenges from internationalization of higher education in GCC countries
GCC youth has benefitted from certain aspects of HE internationalization such as gender equity, a diversified educational landscape offering more choice, and access to global knowledge through English. It has raised the profile of several KSA and UAE universities to rank among the top 500 international institutions (QS world university rankings, 2018). However, it has yielded modest successes in achieving expected economic outcomes. The objective of workforce nationalizationvi remains elusive, and the percentage of citizens employed in the private sector remains insignificant in countries such as Qatar and the UAE (less than 1 and 5% respectively). GCC economies continue to depend on foreign laborers and expatriate professionals for their expanding economic private sector despite government set quota systems and aggressive campaigns to encourage GCC nationals to join the private sector. Business leaders complain that national employees lack the critical, analytical, technical, innovative and communication skills required to lead the knowledge economies of the twenty-first century (Hayes, 2018; Le Haa and Barnawi 2015).vii According to the World bank, '[d]espite large investments in education over the last 50 years, impressive growth in enrollment rates, and gender parity at almost all levels of education, MENA [Middle East and North Africa] has not been able to fully reap the personal, social, and economic benefits of education' (World Bank, 2019, p. ix).
Internationalization has not enabled the region to significantly improve quality and build an 'adequate scientific and technological infrastructure to absorb, apply and create knowledge' (UNESCO, 2018, p. 8). The region continues to be a consumer rather than a producer of knowledge partly due to lack of appropriate funding of research. While GCC nations have heavily invested in education including the provision of significant financial incentives to branch campuses, international partnerships and consultancy services, just about 1% of GDP is allocated to R&D (UNESCO, 2018, p.15). In addition, social constraints on access to data, particularly in the social sciences, do not facilitate conducting research in some parts of the region.
EMI policies have led to social challenges and political tensions with opposition from both progressive and conservative groups in GCC societies.viii Although for different reasons, both sides have decried the low status of Arabic in education. In response, governments have, in some cases, changed course and reinstated Arabic as medium of education in the public universities as is the case in Qatar university following conservative Islamic movements objections. In 2019, the Emir of Qatar signed a law stipulating that 'universities and higher education institutions of the State of Qatar [must] teach in Arabic language and conduct studies and scientific [research] as well in Arabic' (Abdulmalik, 2019). Even branch campuses took steps to respond to other criticisms. Georgetown University's School of Foreign Service in Qatar(SFS-Q), introduced a program in Arabic language teaching for business and media majors to 'expand the ability to read and write in the clearest of Arabic' while studying in English. A similar approach was adopted by UAE public universities (Mahboob & Ilyas, 2017; Badry, 2016; Selvi and Yazan, 2017). However, overall, the push for English continues despite opposition as Barnawi and al-Hawsawi (2017, p. 201) observe in their description of the tensions in KSA.
while Islamic activists have been lobbying government officials in order to block moves to teach English to youngsters as well as adults, business friendly government, neoliberal universities, and corporate bodies, in collaboration with international institutes have been aggressively projecting and imposing English as a "global academic excellence" in order to shape public thinking about its supposed merits in local capacity building.
Many initiatives to protect the Arabic language have not translated into practices in HE. UAE leaders launched the "Arabic Charter" to promote the Arabic language and centers of excellence to develop the use of Arabic in digital technologies and translation in 2012 (Emirates24/7, 2012). And in 2018, a project to create the Arabic Language Academy at UAEU was announced (Ednet, 2018). Bahrain, Kuwait and Oman are relatively late comers to internationalization but even they are not immune to criticism. They have been slower at implementing EMI in their public education system where Arabic remains the main language of instruction but English as a foreign language is being introduced earlier in pre-university (Hayes, 2015).
The GCC region is not the only part of the world having to deal with the dominance of English under globalization. Other non-Anglophone countries in Europe and Asia recognize the hegemony of English in knowledge-based economies and its importance in accessing scientific research and technology. However, they have succeeded in maintaining their mother tongues in education (e.g., French, German, Spanish, Korean, Russian, Chinese, Japanese, etc.) while appropriating the use of English as an added language. In the GCC countries, the embrace of English in the absence of explicit language policies adapted to contextual and linguistic factors has effectively led to the marginalization of Arabic. Socially, 60 percent to 80 percent of the populations are foreigners and English is the lingua franca in business and technical communications. Arabic literacy is a low value commodity on the labor market although it is still the official language. In addition, Arabic is perceived as a difficult language partly due to traditional teaching methodologies that overlook important linguistic properties of Arabic stemming from its diglossic characteristic (Lamine, 2010). Diglossia describes a language where two varieties co-exist side by side in a complementary distribution in a speech community. The Spoken variety of Arabic (SVA) is acquired as the mother tongue used at home and in daily informal communications. The second variety, Modern Standard Arabic (MSA), is learned in school and its mastery depends on its use in education because its function is restricted socially to formal communication and writing. For the teaching of Arabic to be successful, it needs to recognize and address the important linguistic differences between the two varieties (Badry, 2004; Saeigh-Haddad and Schiff, 2016; World Bank, 2019). Yet current teaching methodologies continue to ignore the challenge of diglossia by assuming that the transition from SVA to MSA is automatic. Failure to deal these differences in teaching can generate negative attitudes among learners who perceive MSA to be a difficult language.
Another challenge is in the value accorded to research in Arabic for faculty recruitment and promotion and global university rankings. Major international databases, such as Elsevier's Scopus, Web of Science, Google Scholar, etc., do not index Arabic medium journals resulting in an underrepresentation of research in Arabic on the international scene. Out of an estimated 300 academic journals in Arabic, only two are included in Scopus at present limiting the reach of Arabic publications. As a result, Arab academics have little incentives to publish in Arabic (al hamami, 2015). To compete globally and meet faculty recruitment and promotion requirements, academics must publish in indexed English academic Journals (Barnawi and Al Hawsawi, 2017; Kirkpatrick and Barnawi, 2017). The launch of the first Arabic Citation Index (ARCI), an association between the Clarivate Analytics and the Egyptian Knowledge Bank, projected to start in 2020 may 'facilitate access to Arabic scientific research… [by] enhancing the Arabic academic footprint and ultimately improving university rankings' (Sawahel, 2018).
Internationalization has expanded HE landscapes, but in the absence of long-term strategies that combine modernization with clearly articulated dual language policies, it may end up jeopardizing HE authenticity and independence. EMI policies prolong dependence on the West in teaching and curriculum and slow down the progress of Arabic as a vehicle of knowledge production. They also perpetuate 'a colonised consciousness
where the first language is viewed as somewhat of a handicap rather than a resource to be harnessed' (Phillipson cited in Arfan, 2014, p. 52).
## Conclusion
Internationalization has been embraced in GCC higher education reforms, based on primarily economic objectives, as the shortest means to propel the region into the twenty-first century leading economies. It has benefited the region by improving access and choice, particularly to females whose mobility to the West was limited and who can now pursue higher education at home. It has liberalized education and offered new and multiple delivery modes and opened space for critical inquiry, analysis and innovation. Finally, it has allowed access to worldwide knowledge and economic opportunities. However, despite huge investments and multiple reforms, the returns remain below expected outcomes even when they are measured in economic terms. Linguistically, internationalization, as practiced in the region, has prioritized expediency, through EMI, over building an authentic and sustainable HE that upholds the role of Arabic as affirmed in the GCC countries' visions. In the absence of explicit dual language policies that recognize the contextual and linguistic challenges facing Arabic and spell out ways to deal with them, Arabic is gradually losing ground to EMI in GCC countries' education at all levels. Transplanting educational systems that are disconnected from local socio-historical and political structures, and cultural and linguistic contexts, has limited the benefits of internationalization and created cognitive dissonances between long held beliefs that the Arabian Peninsula is the cradle of Arabic and Islamic identity and the perception that to be part of the knowledge societies of the future, one needs to accept relinquishing one's language and maybe part of one's identity.

## Endnotes
^(i) The distinction public/ non-public institutions is used rather than public/private because even the so called private institutions and branch campuses receive generous support from governments and are subject to varying degrees of state regulations. In addition, some private universities are owned by rulers or members of their entourage.
ii The UAE, with a population of less than 10 million people, has the highest number of branch campuses worldwide with a total of over 180 institutions (Badry, in press, Wilkins, 2010). In KSA, population 33 million, the number of tertiary institutions has jumped from 19 to about 127 and 37 international branch campuses in a decade (Hamdan, 2013). In Bahrain there are 13 non- public institutions for a population of less than 1.5 million. Kuwait has a population of 4.25 million with 4 public institutions and 7 non-public. In Oman, with a population of 4.9 there are 27 non-public universities. These figures are obtained from ministry of education websites of each country. Population estimates are obtained from[ https://www.worldometers.info/world](https://www.worldometers.info/world-population/)[population/](https://www.worldometers.info/world-population/) for each country.
iii One of the desired attributes of the "global citizen" is the ability to communicate well in English.
iv Qatar Foundation, launched in 1995, established the Rand-Qatar Policy Institute (RQPI) in collaboration with the RAND corporation to overhaul the country's educational system including Qatar University which experienced its first major reform in 2003. The reform included the adoption of English as a medium of instruction in most disciplines. Subsequently, the reforms led to major criticisms particularly because they ended up excluding many Qatari citizens from qualifying for admission and at the same time many Qatari faculty members could not teach in English. This led to a reversal in language in education policies with Arabic being reintroduced as a medium of instruction in social sciences and humanities.
^(v) There are other educational free zones in Dubai based on specialty such as the Dubai Health Care city where branches of Western medical schools are established.
vi All GCC economies are powered by 60-80% expatriate workforce primarily in the private sector. This percentage can be as high as 90% in countries such as Qatar. Nationalization- referred to as Emiratization, Saoudization, Qatarization, Omanization, Kuwaitization and Bahrainization- is one of the major goals expected to result from education outcomes.
vii GCC citizens are generally more attracted to public sector employment because of many benefits, such as higher salaries, automatic promotions, longer holidays, shorter working hours and attractive retirement benefits.
viii Conservatives object to English using religious arguments to justify the need to protect from what they perceive as negative influences of Western culture and languages on Islamic societies.
